noteBlocks.lede: Cut a slice out of a pizza and you have a sector: two straight edges and a curved crust. The angle at the centre says what fraction of the whole circle the slice is, and that one fraction gives both the length of its crust and the amount of pizza on it. One idea, used twice.
can: Turn the angle at the centre into a fraction of a full turn.
Work out an arc length as that fraction of the circumference.
Work out a sector area as that fraction of the circle's area.

noteBlocks.md: A sector is a fraction of a circle, and the angle at the centre names the fraction: turn through $90°$ out of $360°$ and you have taken a quarter of the rim and a quarter of the inside. The other pieces have names of their own — a tangent, a chord, an arc, a segment. Nothing in this topic is printed on the Higher formula sheet, so all four circle formulae are memory.

noteBlocks.prompt: A full turn is 360°. What fraction of a whole circle is a 90° sector? Give your answer as a fraction or a decimal.
noteBlocks.explain: Yes: 90 out of 360 is a quarter. Every arc and sector question starts with this one idea.

noteBlocks.md:
A sector is a **fraction of a circle**, and the angle at the centre is what names the fraction. Turn through $\theta$ degrees out of the full $360°$ and you have taken $\dfrac{\theta}{360}$ of everything the circle has: that fraction of the rim, and that fraction of the inside.

So there is really only one formula, used twice:

**Arc length** $= \dfrac{\theta}{360} \times 2\pi r$ — a fraction of the **circumference**.
**Sector area** $= \dfrac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^2$ — the same fraction of the **area**.

Write the fraction first, work out the whole circle second, multiply third. That order keeps the two apart.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which one is the arc length of a sector of radius $r$ and angle $\theta$?
noteBlocks.explain: Yes. An arc is part of the rim, so it grows out of the circumference 2πr. The other line is the sector area, and it would come out in square units.
options: θ/360 × πr²
2πr ÷ θ

noteBlocks.title: Why one fraction does both jobs
noteBlocks.md: Think of the circle as $360$ identical one-degree slivers. Each sliver carries $\dfrac{1}{360}$ of the rim and $\dfrac{1}{360}$ of the inside, so $\theta$ of them carry $\dfrac{\theta}{360}$ of each. That is why the same fraction multiplies the circumference for an arc and the area for a sector.

noteBlocks.title: Nothing here is on the formula sheet
noteBlocks.md:
$C = 2\pi r$, $A = \pi r^2$, arc $= \dfrac{\theta}{360} \times 2\pi r$, sector $= \dfrac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^2$. Four formulae, all from memory.
A quick check on any answer: the arc must be **shorter than the whole circumference**, and the sector area **smaller than the whole circle**.

noteBlocks.prompt: A sector has radius 5 cm and angle 72°. Its arc is $\dfrac{72}{360} \times 2\pi(5)$. What is that, to 1 decimal place?
noteBlocks.explain: 72/360 is one fifth, and one fifth of 31.4159 cm is 6.2832 cm, so 6.3 cm to 1 decimal place.

options: The fraction of the circle, θ/360
The final answer

noteBlocks.text: Perimeter means the whole way round

noteBlocks.md:
A perimeter is the distance round the **outside**, and a sector's outside is partly curved and partly straight. Trace it: out along one radius, round the arc, back along the other radius.

**Perimeter of a sector** $=$ arc $+\ 2r$.

A semicircle works the same way: the curved part is half the circumference, and the straight part is the diameter, so the perimeter is $\pi r + 2r$.

noteBlocks.alt: A sector with both straight edges and the arc drawn, showing the three pieces of the perimeter.

noteBlocks.prompt: A sector has radius 6 cm and an arc of 10 cm. What is its perimeter, in cm?
noteBlocks.explain: Yes: 10 + 6 + 6 = 22 cm. Two radii, because you travel along a straight edge twice.

noteBlocks.title: November 2024, M3 Q20 and M4 Q5
noteBlocks.md:
Both papers asked for the **perimeter of a semicircle**. Most candidates halved the circumference and stopped. Two marks out of three was the typical score.
The fix is not more formulae: it is putting your finger on the diagram and following the edge all the way round before you write the total.

noteBlocks.text: Major or minor: read the diagram

noteBlocks.md:
Two points on a circle give **two** arcs: the short way round (the **minor** arc) and the long way round (the **major** arc). The angle printed at the centre is usually the minor one, so if the diagram draws the long way round you need $360 - \theta$ first.

A free check: the two arcs must add up to the circumference.

noteBlocks.alt: A circle with two radii 100 degrees apart and the long way round from A to B drawn with a thick line.
noteBlocks.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 290' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-labelledby='cs29'><title id='cs29'>A circle with a 100 degree angle at the centre and the major arc drawn thick</title><g fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.1'><circle cx='150' cy='158' r='98'/></g><g fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.4'><path d='M74.9,95 L150,158 L225.1,95'/></g><g fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='3.2'><path d='M225.1,95 A98,98 0 1 1 74.9,95'/></g><g fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2'><path d='M127,138.7 A30,30 0 0 1 173,138.7'/></g><g fill='currentColor'><circle cx='74.9' cy='95' r='2.6'/><circle cx='225.1' cy='95' r='2.6'/></g><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit' font-size='13'><text x='150' y='110' text-anchor='middle'>100°</text><text x='199.3' y='137.4'>r</text><text x='136' y='163'>O</text><text x='62.7' y='88.7' text-anchor='middle'>A</text><text x='237.3' y='88.7' text-anchor='middle'>B</text></g><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit' font-size='11'><text x='6' y='16'>diagram not drawn</text><text x='6' y='29'>accurately</text></g></svg>
noteBlocks.caption: The angle says 100°, but the bold arc is the major one, so it uses $360 - 100 = 260°$.

noteBlocks.prompt: The angle at the centre is 100° and the major arc is wanted. Which angle do you use, in degrees?
noteBlocks.explain: Yes: 360 − 100 = 260. The major arc is everything the marked angle leaves behind.

noteBlocks.md:
On a non-calculator paper you are asked to leave the answer **in terms of $\pi$**. Treat $\pi$ as a symbol you carry through, cancel the fraction first, and never replace it with 3.14.

For a sector of radius 15 cm and angle 24°: the circumference is $30\pi$, the fraction $\dfrac{24}{360}$ is $\dfrac{1}{15}$, and $\dfrac{30\pi}{15} = 2\pi$ cm.

A perimeter then stays as two pieces, for example $(4\pi + 18)$ cm: a multiple of $\pi$ and a whole number cannot be added.

noteBlocks.prompt: A sector of radius 12 cm has an angle of 30°. Write its arc length in terms of $\pi$.
noteBlocks.explain: 30/360 is one twelfth, and one twelfth of 24π is 2π cm.

noteBlocks.md:
Turn the angle at the centre into a fraction of a full turn.
Take that fraction of the circumference for an arc, of the area for a sector.
Add the two radii when a perimeter is asked for.
Use $360 - \theta$ when the major arc is the one drawn.

Expect one three-mark question in the second half of the paper. The first mark is the fraction of the turn together with the right whole-circle formula; the last is the answer rounded exactly as asked, in cm for an arc or a perimeter and cm² for an area. Stuck: work out the circumference or the area of the whole circle anyway — it scores, and it shows which formula the question wanted.

steps.decision: Write the fraction first. A full turn is 360°, so a 140° sector is 140 parts out of 360 of the whole circle — and the arc is that same fraction of the way round the edge.

options: Because the angle at the centre shares the circle out in the same ratio as the edge
Because 360 is the number of degrees in a triangle
Because every sector is a quarter of its circle
whyMenu.explain: Turning through 140° out of a full 360° turn carries you 140/360 of the way around the rim, so the arc is 140/360 of the circumference.

steps.decision: Work out the whole circumference next, and keep the full calculator display. The circle formulae are not on the Higher sheet, so this line has to come from memory.
Multiply by the fraction. Multiplying, not dividing: dividing the circumference by the angle is the error the Summer 2025 report singled out.
Round once, on the answer line, to the accuracy the question names. The unit is a length, so centimetres, not square centimetres.

options: Because an arc is part of the circumference, which is a length
Because all circle answers are in centimetres
Because the radius was given in centimetres squared
whyMenu.explain: An arc is a piece of the rim, so it is measured in centimetres. Square centimetres would mean an area had been found instead.

steps.working: area of the whole circle $= \pi r^2 = \pi(8)^2 = 201.0619$ cm²
steps.decision: Start from the whole circle. The sector will be a fraction of this, and squaring the radius before multiplying keeps the order of operations right.
The same fraction as for an arc. One picture, two uses: the angle shares out the rim for a length and the inside for an area.
Multiply, then round once at the end. Square centimetres, because this is an area.

options: Because the answer measures the surface inside the two radii and the arc
Because every circle answer is in square centimetres
Because the radius was squared, so the unit must be squared
whyMenu.explain: The unit follows what the number measures: a region of surface is in square centimetres. Squaring the radius is part of the method, not the reason for the unit.

steps.decision: Trace the edge with your finger before calculating anything. You travel along one radius, round the arc, and back down the other radius. Every straight edge counts.

options: Because a perimeter is the whole way round the outside
Because a sector always has three sides
Because the radii are the same length as the arc
whyMenu.explain: Perimeter is the distance all the way round. A sector's boundary is curved for part of the way and straight for the rest.

steps.decision: The arc is the same calculation as before. Keep the full display for the addition that follows.
Add both radii. Two radii, not one: 15 cm of straight edge in total.
Round once. If you had stopped at the arc you would have scored the method marks and lost the answer mark, which is exactly what the November 2024 report describes.

workedExamples.stem:
A circle has radius 15 cm. Two radii OA and OB are drawn with an angle of 24° between them.

(a) Find the length of minor arc AB. Leave your answer in terms of $\pi$.

parts.stem: Find the perimeter of the sector OAB. Leave your answer in its exact form.
hints: Add the two radii to the arc.
An exact answer keeps the π term and the whole number apart.
parts.workedSolution: Perimeter $= 4\pi + 9 + 9 = (4\pi + 18)$ cm. Leave it in that form: the two parts cannot be added because one is a multiple of $\pi$.

findTheMistake.stem: Órlaith was asked for the length of the arc of a sector of radius 7 cm with an angle of 260° at the centre, to 1 decimal place. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The circumference is right, and it earns its mark. Line 2 divides by 260 instead of multiplying by 260/360. Dividing would make the arc smaller than the whole rim by a factor of 260, when in fact this sector is most of the circle, so the arc should be most of 44.0 cm.
findTheMistake.feedback: One method mark stands for the circumference. The habit that fixes this is a size check before you write the answer down: a 260° sector is more than half the circle, so its arc must be more than half of 44.0 cm. Summer 2025 M3 Q26 was this exact question type, and dividing by the angle was the error the report named.

findTheMistake.stem: Cara was asked for the perimeter of a sector of radius 9 cm with an angle of 110° at the centre. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The arc is correct and earns both method marks. Line 3 calls the arc the perimeter, but the sector is closed by two straight edges, each 9 cm long, so another 18 cm belongs in the total.
findTheMistake.feedback: Two marks stand: the fraction and the arc are both right. Trace the outline with a finger before you write the total, and say the words out loud: along a radius, round the arc, back along the other radius. November 2024 M3 Q20 and M4 Q5 both lost the same mark on a semicircle.

findTheMistake.stem: Niamh was asked for the length of the major arc AB of a circle of radius 4.5 cm, where the angle AOB marked at the centre is 140°. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The marked angle 140° belongs to the minor arc, the short way from A to B. The major arc is the long way round, so its angle is $360 - 140 = 220°$. Everything after line 1 is done correctly, but on the wrong arc.
findTheMistake.feedback: The arc method is sound, so one mark stands. Before substituting, mark the arc you want on the diagram and ask whether its angle is the one printed or what is left of 360°. A quick check: the two arcs must add to the circumference, 28.3 cm. In Summer 2025 M4 Q12 most candidates gave the minor arc when the major one was drawn.

prompts.prompt: What is the formula for the length of an arc?
prompts.answer: Arc = (θ/360) × 2πr, where θ is the angle at the centre. It is a fraction of the circumference.

prompts.prompt: What is the formula for the area of a sector?
prompts.answer: Sector area = (θ/360) × πr². It is the same fraction of the circle, applied to the area.

prompts.prompt: Are arc length and sector area on the CCEA Higher formula sheet?
prompts.answer: No. Neither is printed, and neither is the circumference or the area of a circle. All four have to be known.

prompts.prompt: How do you find the perimeter of a sector?
prompts.answer: Find the arc, then add both radii. Perimeter = arc + 2r.

prompts.prompt: The angle marked at the centre is 100° but the arc drawn is the long way round. Which angle do you use?
prompts.answer: 260°, because the major arc uses 360 − 100. Check the diagram before substituting; the two arcs add to the circumference.

prompts.prompt: Define a tangent to a circle.
prompts.answer: A straight line that touches the circle at exactly one point. The CCEA Teacher Guidance for M3-GM-01 uses that wording.

prompts.prompt: What is the difference between a sector and a segment?
prompts.answer: A sector is bounded by two radii and an arc, like a slice of pizza. A segment is bounded by a chord and an arc, the piece cut off by a straight line across the circle.

prompts.prompt: How do you find the perimeter of a semicircle?
prompts.answer: Half the circumference plus the diameter: πr + 2r, or (πd/2) + d. The straight edge is part of the outline.

prompts.prompt: A sector answer comes out in cm². What must the question have been asking for?
prompts.answer: An area, not a length. An arc length or a perimeter is in cm; only the sector area is in cm².

prompts.prompt: A sector of radius 15 cm has an angle of 24°. Give the arc length in terms of π.
prompts.answer: 2π cm. The fraction 24/360 is 1/15, and 1/15 of 30π is 2π.

prompts.prompt: You know the arc length and the angle. How do you find the radius?
prompts.answer: Write arc = (θ/360) × 2πr as an equation, then divide by the fraction and by 2π: r = arc × 360 ÷ (θ × 2π).

findings.asked: Length of an arc from its angle.
findings.wentWrong: Many knew the circumference but then divided it by 260 or misused the 100 degree angle; area-based attempts were common; only the best got all three marks.

findings.asked: Length of the major arc drawn on the diagram.
findings.wentWrong: Most found the minor arc (6.1 cm) instead of the major arc (15.9 cm); some forgot to round to 1 d.p.; weaker candidates used area.
findings.rule: Check which arc is drawn: the major arc uses 360 minus the given angle.

findings.wentWrong: Two out of three was typical: the diameter was not added to the arc; a few found the area or used a wrong circumference formula.
findings.rule: Perimeter of a semicircle = half circumference + diameter.

findings.wentWrong: The perimeter formula was chosen correctly but most halved the circumference and stopped.
findings.rule: Perimeter includes every edge, straight ones too.

insight.ruleToRemember: Arc = angle/360 x 2 pi r; sector area = angle/360 x pi r squared; perimeters include the straight edges; check whether the major or minor arc is wanted.
insight.aStarSignal: Working with the major arc or a reflex angle and combining an arc with straight edges in a perimeter.
